summary: We developed Qhalihay (from the Quechua word qhali, meaning healthy), an autonomous health monitoring and clinical decision-support platform designed for long-duration spaceflight. As deep-space missions move beyond Low Earth Orbit toward the Moon and Mars, communication latencies of up to 20 minutes each way make real-time telemedicine from Earth impossible. In these isolated, high-stress environments, astronauts do not need raw medical spreadsheets—they need immediate, actionable certainty under cognitive load. Qhalihay translates complex physiological telemetry, space weather radiation alerts, and daily biometric logs into an interactive 3D anatomical digital twin with a deterministic, server-enforced triage escalation engine. By classifying multi-system health indicators into clear operational states (Normal, Watch, Alert) and assigning exact chain-of-command actions (Self-Care, Crew Medical Officer, or Flight Surgeon), Qhalihay empowers crews to detect anomalies early, execute mitigation protocols in seconds, and maintain crew autonomy without waiting for ground intervention.
details:
1. Detailed Project Description

What exactly does it do?

Qhalihay is an autonomous clinical decision-support system for deep-space crews. Specifically:

  • It replaces complex medical spreadsheets with an interactive 3D anatomical digital twin covering 7 body systems (cardiovascular, brain, metabolic, renal, immune, skeletal, and muscular).
  • It evaluates 13 daily health indicators against official aerospace and clinical standards (NASA-STD-3001, NASA HRP, AHA/ACC, ADA).
  • It automates medical triage escalation (self-care, onboard medical officer, or flight surgeon on Earth) by prioritizing the highest-risk indicator and tracking consecutive days in alert.
  • It measures resting heart rate without external medical devices using only a smartphone's rear camera and LED flash.
  • It provides plain-language physiological explanations, step-by-step action checklists, and an AI medical companion (Orbi) adapted to space communication delays.

How does it work?

  1. Biometric & Space Weather Collection: The astronaut logs 13 daily health indicators (including a 20-second camera pulse check) while the system automatically fetches live solar storm and radiation alerts from NASA DONKI every 30 minutes.
  2. Automated Health Assessment: The server compares each metric against baseline ranges (Normal, Watch, Alert) and assigns an overall status to each organ system using a safety-first, worst-case rule.
  3. Smart Triage Escalation: An automated rule engine assigns action responsibility: the astronaut handles minor changes ("Watch"), the Crew Medical Officer manages immediate alerts, and Mission Control surgeons are notified if an alert persists for two consecutive days.
  4. 3D Anatomical Visualization: The web platform dynamically renders a 3D human body model that updates organ colors directly from server calculations, preventing visual errors or conflicting health states.
  5. Guided Action & AI Support: Tapping any organ displays its function, how spaceflight affects it, and immediate corrective steps, supported by Orbi (an AI assistant grounded in the astronaut's real metrics and mission communication delay).

What benefits does it have?

  • Operational: Eliminates reliance on real-time Earth teleconsultations during 5-to-22-minute Mars communication delays, enabling fast, autonomous medical decisions.
  • Safety & Coordination: Creates a single source of truth with role-based access (Astronaut, Crew Medical Officer, Flight Surgeon, Mission Control), preventing conflicting assessments between crew and ground teams.
  • Logistical & Economic: Uses the crewmember's standard smartphone camera as a pulse monitor, eliminating extra medical hardware, reducing spacecraft payload mass, and allowing one-handed operation in microgravity.
  • Scientific Integrity: Anchors metabolic baselines (glucose, calcium, creatinine) to real pre-flight astronaut data from NASA OSDR (Inspiration4 mission) while clearly labeling simulated demo records.

What do you hope to achieve?

In the short term, our goal is to validate Qhalihay's triage workflow and 3D interface in analog space habitats and remote Earth expeditions where real-time medical support is unavailable. In the long term, we aim to integrate wireless wearable medical sensors and offline edge-AI models so Qhalihay can operate as a standard autonomous medical platform for commercial space stations, lunar bases, and Mars transit crews.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Development Tools: Visual Studio Code, Git, Bun, Docker, Docker Compose
  • Infrastructure and Technological Hosting: Vercel (Frontend), Railway (Backend API & Database), GitHub Cloud
  • Backend & API: Go 1.26, pgx/v5, golang-migrate, JWT Authentication, Server-Sent Events (SSE)
  • Database: PostgreSQL (with role-based access control and embedded migrations)
  • Frontend & UI: React 19, TypeScript 5.9, Vite 8, HTML5, CSS3, Lucide Icons, Custom EN/ES Localization Engine
  • 3D Modeling & Visualization: Three.js, BodyParts3D 4.0 (compressed anatomical meshes), Human-Atlas Viewer
  • Programming Languages: Go, TypeScript, SQL, HTML5, CSS3
  • AI & Machine Learning: Groq API (openai/gpt-oss-120b) with real-time streaming and clinical safety guardrails (Orbi), plus Claude, ChatGPT, and GitHub Copilot for development support
  • Hardware: Standard smartphones (rear camera, LED flash, and haptic feedback for pulse capture) and development workstations
  • Data Sources: NASA OSDR OSD-575 (Inspiration4 metabolic baselines), NASA DONKI API (space weather), NASA-STD-3001, NASA HRP, AHA/ACC, and ADA clinical guidelines
